findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Progress on the 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan and Annual Opinion
findings.headline: Exceptional Hardship Fund exhausted in 2025/26, indicating social pressure on vulnerable residents
findings.detail: The council's hardship fund for Council Tax Support recipients ran out of money during 2025/26 and will only reopen in April 2026. This suggests demand for support exceeded the budgeted provision.
findings.matters: An exhausted hardship fund signals significant social pressures and demand on the council that may indicate wider economic stress in the area affecting council finances. It could also indicate reputational or political risk around support for vulnerable residents.
findings.figures: EHF exhausted in 2025/26; budget timing shows expected reopening April 2026
findings.quote: The SHDC EHF has been exhausted for 2025/26 and will re-open in April 2026.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Progress on the 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan and Annual Opinion
findings.headline: Asset Management Strategy is aged and requires refresh in 2026
findings.detail: The council's Asset Management Strategy is described as 'aged' and will be refreshed during 2026. Currently, the management of the £86.65m property portfolio relies on officers' familiarity rather than being guided by an up-to-date strategy or asset management plan.
findings.matters: An outdated asset management strategy means the council's substantial property portfolio (£86.65m) may not be optimally managed or aligned with corporate priorities. This could affect value realisation and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £86.65m total property value (up from £81.89m in 2023/24)
findings.quote: The aged Asset Management Strategy is to be refreshed during 2026. There is no Asset Management Plan to guide management of individual assets and to ensure alignment with corporate priorities.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Progress on the 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan and Annual Opinion
findings.headline: Debt management has notable weaknesses in aged debt recovery, system use and recovery consistency
findings.detail: The audit identified weaknesses in aged debt recovery, system utilisation and consistency of recovery practice. Management is responding by proposing a dedicated debt recovery officer post, though this is still awaiting approval.
findings.matters: Weak debt management directly impacts cash flow and income collection. Aged debt that is not being recovered reduces the council's cash position. The reliance on a single point of failure increases operational risk.
findings.figures: Weaknesses identified in recovery practice and performance monitoring; proposal for new dedicated officer
findings.quote: There remains a sound underlying system of oversight and debt recovery procedures. However, notable weaknesses remain, particularly within aged debt recovery, system utilisation and consistency of recovery practice and performance monitoring.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Progress on the 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan and Annual Opinion
findings.headline: Dartmouth Ferry service received Limited Assurance due to control weaknesses
findings.detail: One service audit received a Limited Assurance opinion, meaning significant gaps and weaknesses were identified. A new ferry income system is scheduled for June 2026 to address this, with follow-up audit planned.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance is a significant concern showing that control environment in a specific service is inadequate to effectively manage risks. This is the lowest assurance level received (excluding No Assurance).
findings.figures: 1 audit out of 37 completed received Limited Assurance
findings.quote: There has been only one audit with a 'Limited' Assurance (This should be addressed by the introduction of the new ferry income System, scheduled for June 2026, that we will follow up on this year).

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Progress on the 2025-26 Internal Audit Plan and Annual Opinion
findings.headline: Overall control opinion is Reasonable Assurance, not Substantial - meaning identified gaps could affect financial management
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor's opinion is Reasonable rather than Substantial. This means some issues and non-compliance were identified that may put at risk the achievement of objectives. This is a lower level of assurance than the highest category.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand that there are control gaps in the authority's financial governance. Reasonable Assurance indicates room for improvement in risk management and control.
findings.figures: One audit received Limited Assurance; multiple audits received only Reasonable Assurance
findings.quote: There is a generally sound system of governance, risk management and control in place. Some issues, non-compliance or scope for improvement were identified which may put at risk the achievement of objectives in the area audited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Schedule of Capital Programme 2025/26 – Actual expenditure for the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.headline: Three capital schemes exceeded approved budgets in 2025/26, totalling £2,219 of overspend
findings.detail: Follaton House Access Control Upgrades overspent by £1,632 (budget £62,000, actual £63,631.84); Bittaford roof resurfacing overspent by £362 (budget £21,000, actual £21,361.85); pump track design and build overspent by £225 (budget £1,724, actual £1,948.75). While individually small, these represent consistent estimation failures across unrelated schemes.
findings.matters: Repeated overspends indicate project cost estimation or scope management weaknesses that could accumulate across a larger portfolio. Signals to lenders potential cost control issues and to the finance director variable accuracy of project forecasting.
findings.figures: Access Control £1,632 overspend; roof £362 overspend; pump track £225 overspend
findings.quote: Follaton House and Salcombe Access Control Upgrades 62,000 - 62,000 62,000 63,631.84 (1,632)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Schedule of Capital Programme 2025/26 – Actual expenditure for the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.headline: Follaton House Air Source Heat Pump (Salix-funded) concentrated 89% of project expenditure into 2026/27, suggesting delivery slippage or grant funding release delays
findings.detail: A £739,800 Salix-funded decarbonisation scheme, entirely grant-funded, budgeted only £75,000 for 2025/26 (spent £74,335) with the remaining £664,800 scheduled for 2026/27. This marks a significant compression of project activity into the final year.
findings.matters: Year-end concentration of grant-funded activity creates delivery risk and raises questions about whether grant conditions can be met within the grant terms. Matters to lenders concerned with project delivery and grant compliance, and to finance directors managing drawdown timelines and grant clawback exposure.
findings.quote: Follaton House Air Source Heat Pump 739,800 - 739,800 75,000 74,335.00 665 664,800

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Schedule of Capital Programme 2025/26 – Actual expenditure for the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.headline: Local Authority Housing Fund 3 delivered only 56% of budgeted affordable housing expenditure in 2025/26
findings.detail: LAHF 3, funded by government grant and S106 contributions, budgeted £767,483 for deployment in 2025/26 but spent only £431,056.74, leaving £336,426 unspent. Unlike the DFG programme, no remainder was carried forward, meaning funds lapsed.
findings.matters: Underspend on an affordable housing commitment programme raises questions about delivery risk, land availability, or partner capacity on what is typically an outcome-focused grant. Matters to lenders assessing whether the council can execute capital programmes and to finance directors evaluating grant drawdown exposure.
findings.figures: £767,483 budgeted vs £431,056.74 spent (56%); £336,426 undeployed

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Schedule of Capital Programme 2025/26 – Actual expenditure for the 2025/26 financial year.
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant and Renewal Grants severely underspent, with only £623,806 of £1,733,469 deployed in 2025/26
findings.detail: Better Care Grant funding allocated to Private Sector Renewal Grants and Disabled Facilities Grants saw 36% expenditure (£623,805.73) against a £1,733,469 budget, leaving £928,663 unspent and undeployed. Only £181,000 of the remainder was carried forward to 2026/27, meaning the council was unable to utilise 54% of government grant funding earmarked for a core social support service.
findings.matters: Significant failure to absorb and deploy grant funding signals either constrained delivery capacity, demand forecasting errors, or service delivery issues on a means-tested support programme. This matters to lenders assessing financial management rigour and to the s151 officer's ability to execute funded commitments.
findings.figures: £1,733,469 allocated vs £623,805.73 spent (36% uptake); £928,663 undeployed; only £181,000 carried forward
findings.quote: Private Sector Renewal Grants (including Disabled Facilities Grants) 2025/26 allocation 1,733,469 1,733,469 1,552,469 623,805.73 928,663 181,000

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Draft Revenue and Capital Outturn
findings.headline: ICT software and support costs exceeded budget by 25.8% (£188,000 overspend) due to price increases
findings.detail: IT costs overran by £188,000 against a £728,000 budget (25.8%), driven by price increases matching or exceeding inflation and costs for new software licenses and hardware. Like insurance, this reflects market price inflation outpacing budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Systematic inflation pressures across insurance, ICT, and maintenance suggest budget-setting methodology is no longer fit for purpose and recurrent costs are being compressed.
findings.quote: additional costs of £188,000 in respect of ICT software and support contracts in 2025/26. These costs are mainly due to price increases which equal or exceed the inflation rate and additional costs for new software licenses, laptops and accessories.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Draft Revenue and Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Emergency building repairs to Follaton House totalled £85,000, representing a 531% overspend
findings.detail: Repairs to the council's administrative building (roof, sash windows, boiler) cost £85,000 and massively exceeded budget, suggesting either the building was unbudgeted for major maintenance or emergency work was required. This indicates aging asset base and deferred maintenance risk.
findings.matters: The severity of the overspend signals potential maintenance backlog in council-held buildings that could require significant future capital or emergency spending.
findings.figures: Repair cost £85,000 (531.3% overspend)
findings.quote: additional repairs and maintenance costs of £85,000 were incurred in respect of Follaton House in 2025/26. These mainly related to repairs to the roof, sash windows and the boiler.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Draft Revenue and Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Insurance costs overran budget by 39% (£242,000 overspend), driven by inflationary pressures
findings.detail: Insurance expenditure exceeded budget by £242,000 against a £620,000 budget (39% overspend), attributed to inflationary pressures. This sits alongside similar overspends in ICT and other areas, indicating systematic underestimation of cost inflation across the council.
findings.matters: Cost inflation outpacing budget assumptions across multiple service lines suggests future budgets will need material reallocation or cuts unless inflation is reversed.
findings.quote: additional insurance costs of £242,000 were incurred in 2025/26 equating to 39.0% of the total budget of £620,000. This is mainly due to inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Draft Revenue and Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Leisure services contractor Fusion Lifestyle Limited went into administration; council wrote off £500,000 debt
findings.detail: The council's leisure provider entered administration during 2025/26. The council approved a £500,000 write-off in March 2026 to cover debt owed by Fusion. This represents exposure to third-party insolvency risk that has materialized.
findings.matters: Contractor failure indicates service delivery and reputational risk; the £500,000 cost demonstrates material exposure to third-party insolvency.
findings.figures: £500,000 write-off approved March 2026
findings.quote: £0.50 million was used in 2025/26 to fund the write off of debt following the Council's leisure provider, Fusion Lifestyle Limited going into administration. This was approved at Council in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Draft Revenue and Capital Outturn
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending overran by 46.9% due to housing crisis and inadequate DWP subsidy
findings.detail: South Hams budgeted £589,000 for temporary accommodation but incurred an additional £276,000 (46.9% overspend). The council attributes this to factors beyond its control: the housing crisis and lack of available accommodation. The council is attempting mitigation through LAHF property acquisitions, which have avoided over 2,000 nights in less appropriate temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is demand-driven and uncontrollable; overspending at this rate indicates a structural budget pressure that will likely persist and worsen as housing crisis deepens.
findings.figures: Budgeted £589,000; actual overspend £276,000 (46.9%); LAHF investments avoided 2,000+ nights in temporary accommodation
findings.quote: additional expenditure on temporary accommodation over and above what is claimable through the DWP subsidy. This is due to a number of factors beyond the Council's control such as the housing crisis and a lack of accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Summary of Savings and Additional Income 2025/26
findings.headline: IT contract spending overran by £208,000 against a planned £20,000 saving
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £20,000 in savings through IT contract cancellations in 2025/26. Instead, ICT software and contracts overspent by £188,000, resulting in a £208,000 adverse variance (actual: -£208,000 against target of +£20,000). The council attributes the failure to ICT inflationary pressures.
findings.matters: A £228,000 swing from planned saving to actual overspend indicates the council cannot control critical infrastructure spending, and the cited reason (inflationary pressures on external contracts) suggests exposure to cost drivers outside its control
findings.figures: Planned: £20,000 saving; Actual: £208,000 overspend; attributed to £188,000 overrun in ICT software and contracts
findings.quote: This saving was not achieved in 2025/26 mainly due to ICT inflationary pressures. ICT software and contracts were overspent by £188,000 in 2025/26

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for 31 March 2028 introduces material uncertainty to multi-year planning
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly flags that South Hams District Council is scheduled to cease as a separate entity on 31 March 2028 under Local Government Reorganisation. Capital projects and debt schedules extend well beyond this date, creating ambiguity about debt continuity, post-merger servicing, and asset ownership.
findings.matters: Lenders assess borrowing sustainability typically over 20–50 year asset lives; a structural organisational change in 18 months raises questions about how outstanding debt will be managed, who is responsible for repayment, and whether capital assets transfer cleanly.
findings.figures: LGR cessation date: 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The current timetable for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is such that the District Council would cease on 31st March 2028, for modelling and illustration purposes the 2028/29 financial year has continued to be shown.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio carries acknowledged tenant and income risk, with underfunded reserves
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that property investments carry higher risk than treasury holdings due to tenant default, income disruption, and market value volatility. The portfolio was valued at £15.4m as of March 2025. The Maintenance, Management and Risk Mitigation Reserve stands at only £182,000 (March 2026), providing coverage of just 1.2% against asset value—notably modest relative to stated risks.
findings.matters: Commercial property holdings financed by borrowing present credit risk if tenants fail or values fall; inadequate reserves for income disruption create contingency pressure that lenders assess closely.
findings.figures: Investment properties £15.4m (March 2025); MMRM Reserve £182,000; one property held (Dartmouth)
findings.quote: The Council accepts there is a higher risk on property investments than with treasury investments... The Council currently owns one investment property in Dartmouth.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Debt servicing costs rise steeply post-2026/27, climbing from 8.2% of core spending power to 12.5%
findings.detail: Interest and principal repayment (MRP) costs are forecast at £1.26m in 2026/27 (8.2% of core spending), but jump to £1.895m in 2027/28 (12.51%) and stay at £1.887m in 2028/29 (12.61%). This trajectory indicates rising fixed costs will consume an increasing slice of operating budget, constraining flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising debt service as a fixed charge on revenue leaves less room for discretionary spending or reserves; lenders monitor this trajectory as a sign of deteriorating financial flexibility.
findings.quote: Debt servicing (MRP and Interest) as a % of core spending power – £1,260,000/ £15,300,000 = 8.2%

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Total projected debt of £18.933m represents 124% of core spending power—above sustainable thresholds
findings.detail: PWLB debt is forecast to reach £18.933m by March 2027, which exceeds the council's total core spending power (£15.3m) by 24 percentage points. In practice this is manageable, but it places South Hams in the higher-leverage bracket for local government and leaves little margin for income shortfall or service cost increases.
findings.matters: Debt-to-income ratios above 100% signal financial tightness; any shortfall in council tax, business rates, or grants becomes immediately constraining, and lenders use this metric to assess vulnerability to fiscal shock.
findings.figures: Total debt 2026/27 £18,933,000; core spending power £15,300,000; ratio 124%
findings.quote: Total debt (predicted for 26-27) as a % of core spending power - £18,933,000 / £15,300,000 = 124%

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing requirement jumps to £6.632m in 2026/27, nearly five times the prior year
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is forecast at £13.485m in 2026/27, up from £10.937m. External funding covers £2.929m and council resources £3.924m, leaving a net financing need of £6.632m that must be borrowed—compared to only £1.366m in 2025/26. This represents a 385% increase in annual new borrowing in a single year.
findings.matters: Lenders assess a council's capacity to service rising debt; a sudden four-fold increase in borrowing needs signals either rapid capital acceleration or declining internal resources, both of which affect creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 2026/27 net financing need £6,632,000 vs 2025/26 £1,366,000; capital expenditure £13,485,000
findings.quote: Net financing need for the year (This is the prudential borrowing required) 969,000 1,366,000 6,632,000 0 0

findings.paper_title: Month 10 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26
findings.headline: The year-end surplus is critically dependent on investment income that is 37% above budget and may not sustain
findings.detail: Investment income is forecast at £1.37m against a £1m budget—a £370k improvement. This single variance accounts for £370k of the £930k total positive variances achieved. Without this improvement, the council would face a £25k deficit rather than a £345k surplus. The paper notes this reflects interest rates not falling as quickly as predicted and higher returns from longer-term investments. The council has built only £100k of this £370k windfall into 2026/27 budgets, creating a forward risk.
findings.matters: The council's positive financial position depends entirely on asset income that is explicitly contingent on interest rate assumptions. If rates fall or the council's cash balances reduce, this income evaporates, turning the small surplus into a deficit and creating pressure on 2026/27 budgets.
findings.figures: Investment income: budget £1m, forecast £1.37m (+£370k, +37%). This variance alone exceeds the total council outturn by £25k. Only £100k built into 2026/27 budget.
findings.quote: Interest rates have not fallen as quickly as originally predicted in 2025/26. In addition, the Council has been able to secure higher interest rates than originally envisaged through longer term investments.

findings.paper_title: Month 10 Revenue Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Temporary homelessness accommodation costs are escalating significantly and show a worsening multi-year trend
findings.detail: The council spent £429k in 2022/23, £600k in 2023/24, £713k in 2024/25, and projects £799k in 2025/26 against a budget of £589k—a £210k overspend (36%). While the paper acknowledges national pressures (housing crisis, affordability, complex needs), the trajectory is alarming: spending has nearly doubled in three years and the budget is demonstrably inadequate. The council is investing in own housing through LAHF programmes but has not yet achieved stabilization.
findings.matters: This is an uncontrolled structural cost that is escalating despite policy responses. For a lender, it signals a growing liability that could deteriorate further if homelessness demand continues to rise. The council's budget assumptions are fundamentally misaligned with actual need.
findings.figures: 2022/23: £429k actual (£90k over budget). 2023/24: £600k (£261k over). 2024/25: £713k (£374k over). 2025/26 projected: £799k (£210k over budget of £589k, 36% overspend). Three-year spending increase: +86%.
findings.quote: additional expenditure on temporary accommodation of £ 210,000 is currently anticipated in 202 5/26. This is over and above what is claimable back through DWP subsidy and is reflective of the national picture

findings.paper_title: Month 10 Capital Programme Monitoring Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council approving £0.6m external borrowing for Local Authority Housing Fund phase 4
findings.detail: The Executive is reviewing a proposal to acquire four properties under LAHF4, to be funded by £0.7m government grant and £0.6m external borrowing. This represents new council borrowing to support temporary accommodation and resettlement needs.
findings.matters: New external borrowing increases the council's leverage and gross borrowing. Lenders track borrowing decisions and their strategic rationale as indicators of financial management.
findings.figures: £0.6m external borrowing
findings.quote: There is a report on this Executive agenda regarding the opportunity to purchase four properties for LAHF4, utilising £0.7m of Government grant and £0.6m of external borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Total predicted debt for 2026-27 is £18.9m, equivalent to 124% of core spending power.
findings.detail: This includes £1.5m borrowing for Freeport and waste vehicles. All borrowing is at fixed rates (average 2.547%), protecting against interest rate risk. Debt servicing costs (MRP and interest) are 8.2% of core spending power, which is within acceptable thresholds.
findings.matters: Debt at 124% of spending power is above the conventional 100% threshold; while mitigated by fixed-rate protection, this still constrains future borrowing capacity and requires disciplined debt repayment.
findings.figures: Total debt £18.933m vs core spending power £15.3m = 124%; debt servicing £1.26m = 8.2% of spending power; borrowing rate average 2.547%
findings.quote: Total debt (predicted for 26-27) as a % of core spending power - £18,933,000 / £15,300,000 = 124%

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: The council has not yet identified specific solutions to close the projected budget gap for 2027/28 financial year and beyond.
findings.detail: The MTFS shows a budget gap emerging from 2027/28 onwards, but the council has not yet committed to specific savings or income generation measures to close it. Future options will be presented to members in later budget reports.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural budget gaps create medium-term financial uncertainty; a lender needs to understand what service cuts or income measures will be required, and whether these are realistic and achievable.
findings.figures: Budget gap identified for 2027/28 onwards; quantum not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The Council will continue to assess various options for closing the budget gap for 2027/28 onwards

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Council tax income creates above-average financial risk; the council relies on council tax for a higher proportion of its budget than peer councils.
findings.detail: The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index identifies council tax reliance as higher risk than average for peer councils. The budget assumes 650 new Band D equivalent properties per year; if only 450 materialize, council tax income would be £40.5k short.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on council tax (vs other more stable funding sources) increases budget vulnerability to housing market assumptions and collection shortfalls; council tax income is also constrained by government-set referendum limits.
findings.figures: 650 Band D equivalent properties assumed per year, 450 in worst case scenario, resulting in £40.5k shortfall
findings.quote: There is a higher risk around the reliance on council tax income to fund the net revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Income from fees, charges, recycling and investments is material (£14m annually) with identified income volatility risk of £700k if these fall by 5%.
findings.detail: The council budgets £14m from discretionary income sources and identifies that a 5% reduction would cost £700k. This represents meaningful exposure to economic conditions affecting service demand and investment returns.
findings.matters: Discretionary income is vulnerable to economic downturns when council service demand falls and interest rates/market conditions change; a material shortfall would require reserve drawdown or service cuts.
findings.figures: £14m budgeted income, £700k loss from 5% reduction
findings.quote: A 5% reduction in income would result in a loss of £700,000.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus scheme ended in March 2026, removing £0.96m in annual funding that must now be replaced through other savings or income.
findings.detail: This represents a permanent, material loss of revenue that has previously funded the council's operations. The funds can only be replaced through service reductions, additional income generation, or use of reserves.
findings.matters: Loss of established funding sources reduces the council's financial resilience and capacity to service debt; permanent funding gaps require permanent offsetting measures that constrain future flexibility.
findings.figures: £0.96m annual funding loss
findings.quote: The New Homes Bonus Scheme ceased at the end of 2025/26 (representing an annual loss of funding of £0.96m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix H – Sensitivity analysis and risk assessment
findings.headline: Reserve levels are below peer benchmark and will decline further as the council invests £1.5m from earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index identifies South Hams as carrying higher risk than average for both reserve levels and changes in reserves when compared to peer councils. Unallocated reserves of £2.321m represent only 14.5% of the net revenue budget, below the comparator benchmark, and the council is investing £1.5m of reserve funds in Council priorities, further reducing reserves.
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's financial buffer against unexpected pressures; being below peer average and deploying reserves indicates limited capacity to absorb income shocks or service pressures without incurring a deficit.
findings.figures: Unallocated reserves £2.321m (14.5% of net budget), total reserves £9.192m (58% of net budget), £1.5m earmarked reserves to be invested, minimum recommended reserves £1.5m
findings.quote: South Hams has a higher risk than average around its level of overall reserves and a higher risk than average around the change in reserves.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Pension fund valuation shows improvement (100.1% funding), enabling contribution reduction of ~£375,000 per year, providing short-term relief but masking underlying structural pressures
findings.detail: Devon Pension Fund as at 31 March 2025 valued at 100.1% funding level (improved from 98.4% in 2022). South Hams' proportion has 108.3% funding level, creating £9.49m surplus. Actuary has advised contributions can reduce from 20.8% to 16.6% for three years to 31 March 2029. This represents approximately £375,000 annual saving built into budget proposals.
findings.matters: Positive development providing temporary relief (three years only), but masks underlying structural deficit; pension contribution reduction is one-off relief that ends 31 March 2029 and does not address the £2.65m+ budget gaps emerging from government funding cuts
findings.figures: Funding level 100.1%, reduction from 20.8% to 16.6% contributions, saving £375,000 per annum
findings.quote: The actuary has advised that the primary rate contributions of the Council can be reduced from 20.8% to 16.6% for the three years to 31 March 2029. This is a reduction of approximately £375,000 per annum.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Council identified £1.39m of savings for 2026/27 but these only offset £2.49m of cost pressures, leaving shortfall covered by council tax, grants and reserves
findings.detail: Cost pressures total £2.489m (largest: pay award £605k, EPR grant loss £292k, economic development £200k, waste inflation £150k). Identified savings total £1.390m. Combination of council tax increase (2.99%), collection fund surplus (£537k), and reserve contributions make up remaining gap. Reliance on council tax rising faster than income sources indicates growing tax burden on residents.
findings.matters: Savings falling short of pressures indicates council cannot fund cost base from operations; increasing council tax raises burden on local residents and may face political resistance; council is passing cost pressure up the chain rather than absorbing it
findings.figures: Cost pressures £2.489m, savings £1.390m, council tax increase 2.99%, collection fund surplus £537,000
findings.quote: To balance the budget of £ 15.957million, the Council has identified savings and additional income of £ 1.390million.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled for 31 March 2028 creates governance and financial uncertainty during period of peak budget stress
findings.detail: District Council is scheduled to cease on 31 March 2028. Council continues to model 2028/29 'for modelling and illustration purposes' but the council will not exist. Reorganisation creates uncertainty during the very years (2027/28-2028/29) when the council faces largest budget gaps (£2.65m and multi-year cumulative £6.96m).
findings.matters: Reorganization creates dual uncertainty: whether savings strategies are deliverable within a shrinking organization, and whether financial commitments will transfer to successor body; this undermines confidence in medium-term planning
findings.figures: Reorganisation date 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Although the current timetable for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is such that the District Council would cease on 31st March 2028

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Council is using reserve deductions and contribution holidays to balance the current 2026/27 budget, deferring infrastructure maintenance
findings.detail: Ferry Reserve contribution reduced from £177,000 to £50,000 annually. Repairs and maintenance reserve receiving no contributions in 2026/27 despite current balance of only £0.5m (with just £0.2m uncommitted). Council is also drawing £300,000 from Business Rates Retention Reserve to fund 2026/27 revenue budget.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance current-year budgets rather than addressing structural issues indicates underlying inability to match spending to sustainable income; deferral of maintenance spending risks creating larger liabilities later
findings.figures: Ferry Reserve: £177,000 to £50,000; repairs/maintenance reserve £0.5m total (£0.2m uncommitted); £300,000 drawn from Business Rates Retention Reserve
findings.quote: it is recommended to reduce the £177,000 annual contribution to the Ferry Reserve to £50,000 for 26/27. There will be £1m in the Ferry Reserve by March 2026. Similarly it is recommended to not contribute to the repairs and maintenance reserve in 26/27

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Rural funding disadvantage: South Hams residents pay 20% more council tax per head while receiving 41% less government funding than urban areas
findings.detail: Government's Fair Funding Review removed remoteness factor from funding formulas (except adult social care), reduced weighting for visitor/commuter populations, removed separate coastal/flood defence funding formulas, and removed fixed cost adjustment. Analysis by Pixel Financial Management shows rural authorities suffered largest losses in Core Spending Power. RSN analysis shows urban councils receiving 21% funding increase (2024/25 to 2028/29) vs 1% for rural councils.
findings.matters: Council cannot control or offset these funding formula changes; they represent structural disadvantage baked into national policy affecting the council's long-term income trajectory
findings.figures: Rural residents pay 20% (£127) more council tax per head; urban councils receive 41% more government funding per head; urban funding up 21% vs rural 1% (2024/25-2028/29)
findings.quote: For the most rural Councils in the same period, it will have only increased by 1%. In 2026/27, residents in the most rural areas will pay on average 20% (£127) more per head of population in Council Tax than the most urban residents.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset in April 2026 removes all accumulated growth; council has withdrawn from Devon pooling arrangement
findings.detail: First baseline reset since business rates localization began in 2013. Reset removes all accumulated growth from previous years. Safety net set at 100% (meaning council protected at baseline level only). These conditions make Devon pooling uneconomic, so all Devon councils have revoked pooling participation. No pooling gains have been modeled in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Loss of pooling gains and growth income removes discretionary resources previously available; baseline-only funding provides no upside if local business rates growth exceeds government forecasts
findings.quote: The Council has revoked its decision to pool in 2026/27 and all Devon Councils are enacting the same decision.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus scheme ended (annual loss £0.96m) and Extended Producer Responsibility grant reducing by £292,000, compounding income pressures
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus ceased end of 2025/26, removing £0.96m annual funding indefinitely. Separately, DEFRA's Extended Producer Responsibility grant is reducing from £1.025m (2025/26) to £0.733m (2026/27), a £292,000 cut. The council plans to appeal the EPR reduction but has budgeted for the loss.
findings.matters: Loss of discretionary grants reduces the council's flexibility to respond to emerging pressures or protect service quality, particularly as both are permanent or multi-year changes
findings.figures: £0.96m New Homes Bonus annual loss; £292,000 EPR reduction (£1.025m to £0.733m)
findings.quote: It is anticipated that this DEFRA grant will reduce from £1.025m in 25/26 to £0.733m in 26/27 for the new EPR responsibilities. The Council will appeal this reduction in funding.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Unearmarked reserves are forecast to decline to £2.321m by 2027, insufficient to cover the £2.65m 2027/28 budget gap
findings.detail: Total reserves as a percentage of net revenue budget have fallen from 156% (March 2023) to 58% (March 2027 forecast). The council explicitly states it 'may have to use some reserves to potentially bridge any gaps in funding in 2027/28.' With the 2027/28 gap at £2.65m and unearmarked reserves at £2.321m, the council has almost no headroom.
findings.matters: Reserves can bridge temporary gaps but cannot solve structural deficits. A council dependent on reserve drawdown has limited financial flexibility and faces higher risk of breaching minimum reserve requirements or inability to fund contingencies
findings.figures: Reserves 156% (March 2023) to 58% (March 2027 forecast); unearmarked reserves £2.321m; 2027/28 gap £2.65m
findings.quote: the percentage of reserves as a proportion of the Net Revenue Budget has decreased from 156% in March 23 to 58% (predicted) in March 2027

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £2.65m in 2027/28 and £6.96m cumulative by 2028/29 with no identified solutions currently in place
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced, the council explicitly forecasts a £2.65m gap for the following year, described as 'significantly higher than normal at this point in the financial planning cycle.' The cumulative gap by 2028/29 would reach £6.96m if annual gaps are not addressed year-on-year. These gaps are primarily driven by the government funding settlement announced 17 December 2025.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether these gaps can be closed through deliverable savings or whether the council will become dependent on reserve drawdown and further service cuts
findings.quote: The Council is currently forecasting a £ 2.65m budget gap by the following year, 2027/28. The cumulative aggregated Budget Gap by 2028/29 is £ 6.9m

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue and Captial Budget Proposals 2026/27
findings.headline: South Hams faces a 41% reduction in core government funding by 2028/29 and is among the worst-affected councils nationally under the Government's Fair Funding Review
findings.detail: The council has been categorized as one of the most severely impacted in the country. Government funding (Revenue Support Grant and Business Rates baseline) will fall from £6.482m (2025/26) to £3.811m (2028/29). Only 95% of previous funding levels are guaranteed in 2027/28 and 2028/29, meaning no additional funding is available for inflation or service demand despite CPI at 3.4%.
findings.matters: A 41% reduction in a major income source over three years raises fundamental questions about the council's ability to sustain services and meet obligations without fundamental restructuring or significant service reduction
findings.figures: £2.671m reduction (41% decrease), from £6.482m to £3.811m by 2028/29
findings.quote: This is a reduction in Government funding of £2.671m in 28/29 for example – a 41% reduction.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming: Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: Council depleted reserves by £500k in a single year to cover in-year overspends, not one-off items
findings.detail: Despite reporting a £49k surplus for 2024/25, this was only achieved by transferring £500k from the Business Rates Retention Earmarked Reserve. The draw was not for capital or exceptional items but to cover operating overspends—predominantly waste and temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurring operational costs is unsustainable and signals the council is not meeting its recurrent costs from recurrent revenue; this erodes the financial buffer available for unexpected pressures or investment.
findings.figures: £500k transferred from Business Rates Retention Earmarked Reserve in single year
findings.quote: However this surplus position was only achieved after a transfer of £500k from the Business Rates Retention Earmarked Reserve to fund overspends identified in the year, predominantly in the waste service and temporary accommodation costs.

findings.committee: South Hams Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming: Annual Audit Report
findings.headline: Projected budget deficits have grown by 60% in six months as funding settlement cuts deeper than expected
findings.detail: In October 2024 the council identified cumulative three-year deficits of £3.9m. When setting the 2025/26 budget in February 2025, this grew to £6.3m—a £2.4m increase driven primarily by announced reductions in Rural Services Delivery Grant and New Homes Bonus. The 2026/27 deficit alone jumped from £1.1m to £3.4m.
findings.matters: Rapidly widening deficits signal structural funding loss rather than one-off pressures; lenders need clarity on whether existing savings plans can bridge a gap that has already doubled, and whether reserves are adequate given the trajectory.
findings.figures: Cumulative gap £3.9m (October 2024) rising to £6.3m (February 2025); 2026/27 deficit increased from £1.1m to £3.4m
findings.quote: The budget gap for 2026/27 has increased significantly from the October 2024 update due to the Local Government Finance Settlement announcement for 2025/26.
